other_side: Zitron's June 30 piece reads the AI-and-work story as a con running in both directions. Agents marketed as autonomous actually chain people to longer hours — he cites Bloomberg's account of engineers working until 4am alongside the bots they deploy, and a founder who says he has "never worked harder in my life." The replacement threat, meanwhile, is deliberate fear-marketing by labs whose models, he writes, "cost about as much as a person" yet can neither replace one nor turn a profit, with benchmarks "rigged in their favor." On his account, hiring data from AI-heavy firms would show only that the tools demand ever more human supervision.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether AI, at today's capability, complements human labour or substitutes for it. Both accept more than they let on: NLW's own headline benchmark has AI completing just 16 per cent of freelance tasks to professional standard, and Zitron insists models cannot replace a person — so both agree the substitution case is currently weak. The empirical question that will resolve is whether headcount at high-AI-adoption firms keeps growing as the tools mature; the observable that settles it is the next rounds of payroll data — Ramp and Revelio follow-ups, and the BLS tech-and-finance series — through 2027. The residue is pure worldview: whether higher output per worker is liberation or exploitation. NLW is vindicated if hiring growth persists and broadens beyond the subsidised early adopters; Zitron if it proves a spending artefact that reverses when the cheap money stops. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW sells daily optimism, Zitron sells bubble certainty — so the signal is their overlap: today's AI does a small fraction of real work. Watch the next Ramp/Revelio update against the 28,000-a-month tech job losses.
